a: the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah
p: Zedekiah's tenth year and Nebuchadnezzar's eighteenth overlap in 587 BC, with the city's fall still under two years away.
b: Zedekiah took the throne in 597 BC. Counting years from the autumn new year, as many scholars do for Judah's kings, his tenth year is 588/587 and his eleventh, in whose fourth month the city fell (2 Kings 25:2–3), is 587/586. That puts the fall in the summer of 586 BC, the date this site uses; some scholars say 587. Babylonian years began in the spring. Nebuchadnezzar became king in 605, and if his years are counted from his first full year (604), his eighteenth is 587/586, so the two counts overlap from spring to autumn of 587. Scholars explain small gaps like this by the two ways of counting a king's first year, from his accession or from the next new year, which also lie behind other date puzzles in Jeremiah (compare 52:12, 29). Either way the Babylonian army is outside the walls and the city has under two years left.

a: shut up in the courtyard of the guard
p: Jeremiah is under guard but not in a cell: family, friends and scribes can reach him.
b: The courtyard of the guard was a yard in the palace grounds where a prisoner was kept under watch. It was far milder than the cistern dungeon of 37:16. Here Jeremiah receives his cousin, hands a deed to Baruch before witnesses and is later questioned by the king (38:14). The events of chapters 32 and 33 fall after Zedekiah moved him here from the house of Jonathan (37:21) and before the city fell (38:28).

t: Eyes to eyes, mouth to mouth
p: Zedekiah will meet the king of Babylon face to face. It comes true at Riblah.
b: The Hebrew says his mouth will speak with the king's mouth and his eyes will see the king's eyes. When it happened, the Babylonian king judged Zedekiah at Riblah, killed his sons while he watched, and then put out his eyes (2 Kings 25:6–7). The last thing Zedekiah saw was his sons' deaths. See 34:3 for the same words, and 38:23 for the warning that his family would be taken out first.

a: until I turn my attention to him
p: The verb can mean visit for good or for harm, and the verse does not say which.
b: Paqad means to turn attention to someone: to visit, count, check on or call to account. In 29:10 the LORD uses it for good (he will turn his attention to the exiles and bring them home). Elsewhere it is used for judgment (6:15). Here Zedekiah stays in Babylon until the LORD visits him. Jeremiah 52:11 says he was kept in prison there until the day he died, which fits a visit that means his death. Others read the verb as a hint of mercy.
orig: פָּקַד (paqad), 'visit, attend to, call to account'

a: the right of redemption is yours
p: Family land had to stay in the family. The closest relative had the first right to buy it back.
b: Leviticus 25:25 says that if a man becomes poor and sells some of his holding, "his closest family redeemer is to come and buy back what his brother sold." Ruth 4:4–6 shows the practice at work. Hanamel, Jeremiah's cousin, has to sell, and the field lies in Benjamin, where the Babylonian army is at work. Jeremiah's family were priests of Anathoth (1:1). To buy was to keep the field in the clan and, as the LORD uses it, to promise that the clan will be there to keep it.

a: just as the LORD had said
p: Jeremiah knew the strange order was from the LORD only when his cousin arrived with the offer.
b: The LORD had told Jeremiah in 32:7 that Hanamel would come, and then Hanamel came. That small fulfilment let Jeremiah know that the odd order to buy a field in a district held by the enemy was truly the LORD's. It is the test of a prophet that Deuteronomy 18:22 describes, here applied to Jeremiah himself. Only after this does he act, and his prayer in 32:16–25 shows he still found the order hard.

p: The Hebrew says 'seven shekels and ten of silver', which the Plain counts as seventeen shekels. Radak and the Targum read larger units.
b: The Hebrew text reads "seven shekels and ten the silver." Read plainly this is seventeen shekels of silver, and the Plain keeps that. Radak reads it differently: the "shekels" are minas and the "silver" is selas, and he adds that Targum Jonathan translates it the same way ("seven minin and ten selain of silver"). So the medieval Jewish reading is of much larger units. If the sum is seventeen shekels, it is a low price: Abraham paid four hundred shekels for a field and cave at Hebron (Genesis 23:15–16). A low price might suit a time of war, a small plot, or a sale between relatives, but the text gives no reason, and larger units would need none. The Greek has the same words as the Hebrew.

a: I weighed the silver on a balance
p: There was no coined money in Judah in 587 BC. Payment was silver weighed on scales.
b: Buyers in Jeremiah's day paid in pieces and scraps of silver weighed against stone weights. Coins were first struck in western Asia Minor in the 600s BC and did not come into use in Judah until later. That is why the story names the witnesses and the scales together: the weighing was the payment, and the witnesses were the proof. Stone weights marked with the shekel and its fractions have been found in Judean towns.

t: A sealed copy and an open copy
p: The deed was written twice: one copy rolled, tied and sealed against changes, the other open for reading.
b: The Hebrew calls them "the sealed one" and "the open one." Contracts with the same text sealed and open are known from the ancient Near East. The sealed copy protected the terms against changes, and a judge could break it open to check the open one. The terms are called hammitsvah vehaqqim, here "the instructions and the conditions." Swete's Greek mentions only the sealed copy at this verse, though it knows both copies in 32:14.

p: The Hebrew word is the one later translated 'the Jews'. Here it simply means people of Judah.
b: Yehudim is an old word for people of the kingdom of Judah (compare 34:9; 38:19; 40:11–12; 2 Kings 25:25). It does not yet mean followers of the later Jewish religion. This book renders it "Judeans" wherever it means people of the land of Judah. Older English Bibles say "the Jews who sat in the courtyard of the guard," because the Hebrew, Greek and Latin words are the same as the ones for the later Jewish people.

a: Baruch son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah
p: Baruch, the scribe who writes Jeremiah's scroll, appears for the first time, as the keeper of the deeds.
b: Baruch came from a family of officials. His brother Seraiah, a quartermaster, carried Jeremiah's word to Babylon (51:59). In chapter 36 Baruch writes the scroll and reads it in public. Here Jeremiah gives him the deeds and one order: put them in a jar. For the clay seal impression that names a Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe, and the debate about it, see 36:4.

a: The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel
p: The title pictures God as commander of armies: of Israel, of angels and of the stars.
b: Yahweh tseva'ot appears over eighty times in Jeremiah. "Armies" may mean Israel's armies, the angels or the stars (compare 33:22, "the army of the heavens"). The title suits the chapter: the God who commands every army hands the city to Babylon (32:28) and promises to bring the people back (32:37). The Greek often renders it "the Lord Almighty" (Pantokrator) and sometimes has no title where the Hebrew has this one.

a: put them in a clay jar
p: Clay jars were used to keep documents for a long time.
b: Clay jars with a lid kept papyrus and leather dry. The best-known example is the Dead Sea Scrolls, many of which were found in jars in the caves. Jeremiah's order shows he expected the deeds to be needed after a long gap ("many days"), by people living again in the land. The jar is the sign: the deed is put away, not thrown away.

t: A deed for a ruined land
p: Jeremiah's purchase is a promise acted out before the city falls.
b: Jeremiah told the exiles to build houses and plant gardens in Babylon (29:5) and now buys a field at home. The two acts belong together: the people will be taken out and will be brought back. The deed in the jar says the land has not been taken from them for good. Prophets often acted out their messages (13:1–11; 19:1–13; 27:2). This one acts out a hope, and it uses an ordinary legal sale.

p: The Hebrew is the word for God's wonders. Many Bibles say 'too hard'.
b: The verb yippale' comes from the root for "wonderful, extraordinary" (pele'), used of the miracles of the exodus. The same word is in Genesis 18:14: "Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?" That was said to Sarah when she laughed at the promise of a son. Jeremiah brings it into his prayer, and in 32:27 the LORD says it of himself. Luke 1:37 and Matthew 19:26 are often compared. The Greek of both verses reads "hidden" (see the variants).

a: repay the guilt of the fathers into the laps of their children
p: The prayer quotes an old saying about God's judgment on later generations, which Jeremiah elsewhere says will end.
b: The wording comes from Exodus 34:6–7 and Deuteronomy 5:9–10: God shows loyal love to thousands and holds later generations to account. Jeremiah quotes it as praise. Yet in 31:29–30 he says the people will no longer quote the proverb about sour grapes and children's teeth, and Ezekiel 18 argues the same. Lamentations 5:7 puts both thoughts side by side: "Our ancestors sinned, and they are gone; / we are the ones who carry their guilt." In this chapter the city really is paying for generations of sin (32:30–32).

a: with a strong hand and an outstretched arm
p: The prayer recites the standard words about the exodus from Deuteronomy.
b: The phrase is almost the same as Deuteronomy 26:8: "with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, with great terror, with signs and with wonders." (Deuteronomy 4:34 has the plural, "great terrors.") It comes from the creed Israel recited with its first fruits and is the praise Jeremiah offers before he complains. The prayer follows the creed's order: what God has done (32:17–22), what Israel did (32:23), and the present trouble (32:24–25). The Greek of Jeremiah has "great visions" here; the Greek of Deuteronomy 26:8 and 4:34 has the same words for the same Hebrew phrase (see the variant).

a: did not walk in your law
p: Torah means teaching or law. In Jeremiah it is the teaching God gave Israel to walk in.
b: Torah is the LORD's "teaching," and in this verse the law Israel was to walk in. Jeremiah complains that people have the torah and do not keep it (6:19; 8:8; 9:13). In 26:4 the LORD uses the same words as here: "to walk in my law that I set before you." The Plain uses "law" for this sense. The land was given on the condition of walking in it (Deuteronomy 4:1; 30:15–20).

p: A ramp of earth and rubble was built against a wall so that soldiers and battering rams could climb it.
b: The Hebrew solelot are heaps or ramps piled up against a city wall. The ramp Sennacherib built against Lachish in 701 BC can still be seen, and Assyrian carvings show soldiers climbing such ramps. Isaiah 37:33 promised that Assyria would not throw up a siege ramp against Jerusalem. Now Babylon does. The Greek has "a crowd" here, as if it read a different word (see the variants).

p: The LORD answers Jeremiah's doubt by saying who he is: God of every living thing.
b: "All flesh" means every living creature and above all every human being (Genesis 6:12–13; Isaiah 40:5–6). The title is rare; Numbers 16:22 and 27:16 have "God of the spirits of all flesh." The claim is wide on purpose. Jeremiah has asked how God can order a purchase while Babylon takes the land (32:25). The answer is who God is: the one who gives the city to Nebuchadnezzar (32:28) also decides the future of the land.

p: Flat roofs were used as shrines for incense to Baal and the stars.
b: People burned incense and poured out drink offerings on flat rooftops, to Baal and to the "army of heaven" (the stars). Zephaniah 1:5 names the practice, and 2 Kings 23:12 says Josiah pulled down altars on the roof. Jeremiah 19:13 repeats the charge for Jerusalem's houses, and the women in Egypt defend it in 44:17. Here the punishment is aimed at the very houses where the incense went up.

p: The Hebrew idiom means doing something eagerly and again and again.
b: The idiom hashkem, "getting up early," is a favorite of Jeremiah (7:13, 25; 11:7; 25:3–4; 26:5; 29:19; 35:14–15; 44:4). The LORD is pictured as a teacher or a sender of messengers who starts the day early. The charge is not that Israel lacked a teacher but that it "would not listen and take correction" (musar).

t: Passing sons and daughters to Molech
p: The verse does not say 'through the fire'. Other texts do, and scholars differ on what happened.
b: The Hebrew says only "to make their sons and their daughters pass over to Molech." 2 Kings 23:10 adds the fire: "so that no one would ever again make his son or his daughter pass through the fire for Molech." Jeremiah 7:31 and 19:5 speak of burning sons in the fire. Some scholars think the rite was dedication by fire; others think children were killed. Some link the Hebrew word Topheth to the burial grounds called tophets at Carthage, which hold the burned bones of small children. The Greek reads "Molech the king."

a: it never came into my heart
p: Jeremiah says God never commanded child sacrifice. Ezekiel seems to say God gave bad rules.
b: In 7:31, 19:5 and here the LORD says that burning children "never came into my heart." Exodus 22:29 says the firstborn son is to be given to the LORD, and Ezekiel 20:25–26 says God gave "rules that were not good" and made the firstborn pass through the fire. Readers have explained this in several ways: God never commanded the sacrifice and Ezekiel speaks in bitter irony; God let Israel follow the custom as a punishment; or the Exodus law meant the redemption of the firstborn (Exodus 13:13), not sacrifice.

a: I am gathering them from all the lands
p: The promise of a gathering repeats Moses' promise in Deuteronomy.
b: Deuteronomy 30:3–4 says the LORD will gather the scattered people from every nation where he has driven them. Jeremiah repeats it for the exiles (29:14; 31:8, 10) and in 23:3, 8. In this chapter the promise is given on the same day the city is told it will fall, which is why the deeds are put in a jar.

a: They will become my people, and I will become their God.
p: 'My people, your God' is the short form of the covenant promise.
b: The formula occurs through the Bible: Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 24:7; 30:22; 31:33; Ezekiel 36:28; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Revelation 21:3. In 31:33 it follows the law written on the heart; here the next verses fill it out (one heart, fear of God, an everlasting covenant). The clause order is Hebrew: "they will become to me a people, and I will become to them God." It is a promise of belonging, said to a people about to lose their land.
r: Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:28; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Revelation 21:3

p: The people will no longer be divided in what they love and how they live. The Greek says 'another'.
b: The Hebrew has lev echad, "one heart," and derekh echad, "one way." The Greek has "another way and another heart," which may reflect the easy slip between the Hebrew letters dalet and resh (echad, "one," and acher, "another"). Ezekiel 11:19 and 36:26 promise a "new" heart, and the promises are often read together. "One heart" means a heart undivided in loyalty, the opposite of the "stubborn and rebellious heart" of 5:23.
orig: לֵב אֶחָד וְדֶרֶךְ אֶחָד (lev echad vederekh echad)

t: The everlasting covenant and the new covenant
p: The 'everlasting covenant' here sounds like the new covenant of 31:31–34.
b: Jeremiah speaks of "an everlasting covenant" (berit olam) here and in 50:5. Ezekiel 16:60 and 37:26 and Isaiah 55:3 and 61:8 use the same phrase. Many commentators treat 32:38–41 as the same promise as 31:31–34, spoken now to people in a siege: the same fear of the LORD, and the same "I will put" (31:33; 32:40). Christian readers connect it with the new covenant of the Lord's Supper and Hebrews 8; Jewish readers see a covenant with Israel in its land.
r: Jeremiah 31:31–34; Jeremiah 50:5; Ezekiel 16:60; Ezekiel 37:26; Isaiah 55:3; Hebrews 8:8–12

a: with all my heart and all my being
t: God plants with the whole heart
p: Israel was told to love God with all its heart and being. Here God plants Israel with all of his.
b: Deuteronomy 6:5 commands Israel to love the LORD with all its heart and being, and Josiah is praised for turning to him "with all his heart and all his being" (2 Kings 23:25, "with all his heart, with all his being"). Here the phrase turns around: the LORD plants his people "with all my heart and all my being." The word for "being" is nefesh, a person's life or self. Few verses say so strongly that God puts himself into a promise.
orig: בְּכָל לִבִּי וּבְכָל נַפְשִׁי (bekhol libbi uvekhol nafshi)

p: The phrase shav shevut was long read as 'bring back the captivity'. Many now take it to mean restore.
b: The idiom is shuv shevut (or shevit) in Jeremiah 29:14; 30:3, 18; 31:23; 32:44; 33:7, 11, 26; 48:47; 49:6, 39. The KJV follows the Hebrew word shevut and the Greek and says "bring again the captivity." Because the phrase is used of Job (Job 42:10) and of nations that were not taken captive, many scholars take it to mean "restore the fortunes." Here the whole land, and not only the exiles, has its fortunes turned around.

p: The six regions named here are the map of the restored land.
b: Benjamin (north), the area around Jerusalem, the towns of Judah, the hill country, the Shephelah (the low hills between the hill country and the coast) and the Negev (the dry south) cover the whole kingdom of Judah. The same list opens 17:26 and returns in 33:13. Land is again bought and sold in every region, so the promise is for all of Judah and not only for Anathoth.

t: The second word in the courtyard
p: This word comes to Jeremiah in the same place and time as chapter 32.
b: "A second time" joins this chapter to chapter 32: Jeremiah is still shut up in the courtyard of the guard (32:2). Chapters 32 and 33 are the largest block of hope in the part of the book that tells about the siege. The Greek has the first half of this chapter (33:1–13) but not 33:14–26.

p: 'It' has no noun. The Greek supplies 'the earth'.
b: The Hebrew oseh has a feminine ending, "who made it," and does not say what "it" is. The Greek reads "the LORD who makes the earth and forms it." Others take "it" to be Jerusalem or the plan the LORD is about to describe. The phrase "made it... formed it... set it firm" sounds like Isaiah 45:18, which speaks of the earth. Whether earth or city, the LORD names himself as the maker before he gives his promise.

p: The Hebrew word means shut away or guarded, not 'unsearchable'. The promise was made to a prisoner in a siege.
b: Betsurot can be derived in two ways. Some link it to batsar, "cut off, make inaccessible, fortify," so shut-away or fortified things. Others link it to natsar, "guard, keep," the root of netsurot, "guarded things," in Isaiah 48:6, where the LORD also tells of new things "that you did not know." Either way the word means things kept back until now. The KJV has "great and mighty," and the Greek has "great and strong things" (see the variant). The verse is often used as a promise that God will answer any prayer. Its first hearer was a man locked in a courtyard while his city was destroyed, and the "hidden things" are the promises in 33:6–26. The call-and-answer pattern appears elsewhere (Psalm 91:15; Isaiah 65:24).

a: pulled down because of the ramps and because of the sword
t: Houses torn down for the defense
p: Houses were pulled down to get stone and to make room for walls. The Hebrew is short and hard.
b: The Hebrew says houses that "have been pulled down because of the ramps and because of the sword." The usual explanation is that houses were pulled down to get stones to strengthen the wall against the ramps, as in Hezekiah's day: "You made a list of Jerusalem's houses and pulled some down to shore up the wall" (Isaiah 22:10). Another is that the enemy's ramps and weapons smashed the houses. The line may mean both.

a: People are coming to fight the Chaldeans
p: The sentence has no stated subject, and translators supply different ones.
b: Literally: "coming to fight with the Chaldeans and to fill them with the corpses of the people whom I struck down." Three readings: (1) the Judeans go out to fight and the houses fill with their dead; (2) the Chaldeans are the ones coming, and the houses fill with bodies of those the LORD struck down; (3) the text is damaged. The Greek (40:5) has the same difficulty. The Plain keeps the Hebrew order and leaves the subject open.

p: The healing Jeremiah has been asking for in the book is promised.
b: Jeremiah cried out earlier, "Is there no balm in Gilead? Is no healer there?" (8:22) and the people say there is no healing for them (14:19). In 30:17 the LORD says he will bring healing. Here the answer comes in two words, arukah and marpe, both meaning healing (the first is the new flesh that closes a wound). It is given to the same city that 33:4–5 describes as full of corpses.

a: I will forgive all their guilt
p: The verb salach is used in the Bible only when God is the one forgiving.
b: Salach has God as its subject every time it appears in the Old Testament. People "pardon" with other verbs. The verse piles up three words for wrongdoing (guilt, sinning, rebelling) and two for what God does (cleanse, forgive). Compare 31:34: "I will forgive their guilt." The promise of forgiveness here comes before the promise of a king and priests.

a: a name of joy, a praise and an honor
p: The three words repeat what Israel was meant to be for God, as in Deuteronomy.
b: Moses said the LORD would set Israel high above the nations "for praise and fame and honor" (Deuteronomy 26:19), and Jeremiah 13:11 says Israel was meant to be "my people, my name, my praise and my honor", but would not listen. Here the city becomes a name, praise and honor, and the nations who see the good done to it "will be in awe and tremble." The reputation of Israel and the reputation of God cannot be separated here.

a: the sound of the groom and the sound of the bride
p: In 7:34, 16:9 and 25:10 the LORD took these sounds away. Here he gives them back.
b: Three earlier passages say the sound of the groom and the bride will stop in Jerusalem and Judah (7:34; 16:9; 25:10). This promise reverses them. Revelation 18:23 uses the same line against Babylon, and John 3:29 speaks of the bridegroom's voice. The sounds of joy are joined to the thanks of worshippers, so that weddings and temple worship both return.

p: The words the people will say are the standard thanksgiving formula of the temple.
b: "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his loyal love is forever" is the refrain of Psalm 136 and the opening of Psalms 106, 107 and 118. It was sung at the dedication of Solomon's temple (2 Chronicles 5:13; 7:3) and when the foundation of the second temple was laid (Ezra 3:11). The "thank offering" (todah) is the sacrifice that goes with such a song (Psalm 107:22; 116:17).

a: the good word that I spoke
t: The passage missing in the Greek
p: Verses 14 to 26 are not in the Old Greek. A Qumran Hebrew copy has parts of 16 to 20.
b: The Old Greek of Jeremiah, about one-seventh shorter than the Hebrew, lacks all of 33:14–26. Scholars who hold that the Greek translates an earlier edition of the book think the passage was added to the Hebrew later; those who hold that the Greek abridged its source think the translator left it out. Fragments of 33:16–20 survive in a Qumran scroll (4QJer-c), so the passage was in some Hebrew copies before the Common Era. That does not settle how old it is. See the variants at each verse.

p: This is the promise of 23:5–6. The Jewish and Christian readings differ on who the Branch is.
b: The Hebrew is tsemach tsedaqah. In 23:5 it is tsemach tsaddiq, "a righteous Branch." Tsemach is a sprout from a cut-down tree (Isaiah 11:1) and is a name for the coming king in Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12. The Aramaic Targum of Jeremiah renders it "Messiah of righteousness" (meshiha ditsdqa), and Radak links the Branch with the Messiah. Christian readers see Jesus (Luke 1:78, where "dawn" is the Greek word the Greek Old Testament uses for the Branch in Zechariah 3:8). Critical scholars connect the language with the hope placed in Zerubbabel (Zechariah 3:8; 6:12). The Plain words 33:15–16 as 23:5–6 wherever the Hebrew is the same ("carry out justice and righteousness in the land," "Judah will be saved," "settle in security").
r: Jeremiah 23:5–6; Isaiah 11:1; Isaiah 4:2; Zechariah 3:8; Zechariah 6:12; Luke 1:78

a: This is what one will call her
t: Whose name is 'The LORD is our righteousness'?
p: In 23:6 the name belongs to the king. Here the pronoun is feminine, so it is the city's.
b: In 23:6 the Hebrew reads "this is his name by which he will be called," so the king carries the name. In 33:16 the Hebrew is shorter: "this is what one will call her." It has no word for "name" and no stated subject, and the pronoun is feminine, so Jerusalem carries the name. The Plain keeps the unstated subject with "one will call her"; the other way to put it is "this is what she will be called." Radak says God will call Jerusalem by this name, and he also connects the name with the Messiah. He cites the Targum, which ties the name to merits before God. Whichever way it is read, the name shifts from the king to the city, so that the whole community is called by the LORD's righteousness.

a: David will never be without a man sitting on the throne
t: A throne that is never empty
p: The promise of an unbroken Davidic line stands beside the fact that the throne was empty after 586.
b: The promise echoes the dynasty promise to David (2 Samuel 7:16; 1 Kings 2:4; 8:25). Jeremiah said no son of Jehoiachin would sit on David's throne (22:30), and the throne was in fact empty after 586. Jewish readers place the fulfilment in a future king of David's line. Christian readers see Jesus as the descendant who reigns forever (Luke 1:32–33). Critical scholars date the promise after the exile, when hope for a king lived without a king. The end of 2 Kings shows a Davidic prince still alive in Babylon (25:27–30).

p: The phrase comes from Deuteronomy. The promise puts priests and king on equal footing.
b: Hakkohanim halwiyyim, "the Levite priests," is the phrase of Deuteronomy (17:9, 18; 18:1; 24:8), where it covers the priests of the whole tribe of Levi. Ezekiel 44:15 uses the same words but limits them: "the Levite priests, the sons of Zadok." So the phrase is shared, and the question is how wide it is drawn: Deuteronomy and Jeremiah apply it to the whole tribe, Ezekiel to Zadok's sons alone. The promise pairs the priests with the king, and both are tied to the covenant of 33:20–22. A priesthood forever (compare Numbers 25:13 for Phinehas) became a problem for readers after AD 70, when sacrifices stopped. Jews and Christians have read the promise differently; see the card on this page.

a: my covenant with the day and my covenant with the night
t: A covenant with day and night
p: The regular order of day and night is called a covenant, as after the flood.
b: Genesis 8:22 promises that day and night, summer and winter will never stop as long as the earth lasts, and Genesis 9:9–17 calls the promise to Noah a covenant with every living thing. Jeremiah 31:35–37 uses the same argument: the sun, moon and stars are fixed, and so is Israel. Here the covenant with David and Levi is as certain as the cycle of day and night. The word "covenant" for the order of creation is rare, and some scholars therefore speak of a creation covenant.

p: Numbers like the stars and the sand were promised to Abraham. Here they are promised to David and Levi.
b: "Army of the heavens" means the stars (compare Genesis 15:5: "Look toward the sky and number the stars, if you can number them"). "Sand of the sea" is from Genesis 22:17 and 32:12. The promise of countless offspring to Abraham is now given to the royal and priestly lines, and 33:26 names all three patriarchs. The same "army of heaven" was worshiped in 8:2 and 19:13. Here it is only a measure of how many God will make.

p: The text does not say which two clans are meant, and readers have chosen several pairs.
b:
Radak says the two clans are the family of David and the family of Aaron, the king and the priests of 33:17–22, and that the people look down on their leaders when they see them rejected. Another reading takes the pair from 33:14, "the house of Israel and the house of Judah", so the two kingdoms. A third takes it from 33:26, "Jacob and David." The people who say this may be foreigners who despise Israel, or the exiles themselves, who feel rejected.

Verses 24–26 are also used in the debate over whether God has rejected Israel (compare Romans 11:1–2, 29). The Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate (1965, section 4) says the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God; other churches read the passage in other ways, and the topic page sets the views out.

a: rulers over the offspring of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
p: The closing verse names the three fathers and ties the promise to them.
b: The verse puts "Jacob and David" together and names "Abraham, Isaac and Jacob" as the people over whom David's line rules. The three names are those of the God of the fathers (Exodus 3:6) and the foundation of the land promise. Jeremiah 31:37 makes a similar argument from the heavens and the earth's foundations. The closing words, "I will turn their fortunes around, and I will have compassion on them," echo 30:3 and 30:18.

p: Zedekiah did not die by the sword, but 2 Kings and Jeremiah 52 say he was blinded and kept in prison in Babylon.
b: The promise sits beside what happened: he saw his sons killed, was blinded and died a prisoner (2 Kings 25:7; Jeremiah 39:6–7; 52:11). Readings: (1) "in peace" means only not by the sword, as in 34:4; Radak says he would die on his bed and receive the honors due to kings, and he adds the saying of the Sages that Nebuchadnezzar died in Zedekiah's lifetime. (2) The promise was conditional on his obeying (compare 38:17–18 and 18:7–10), and he did not obey. (3) Critical scholars hold that the prophecy was not fulfilled as spoken. Josephus says Zedekiah died in prison in Babylon (Antiquities, book 10).

a: As burnings were made for your fathers
p: Spices or a great fire were burned at a king's funeral. Zedekiah is promised the same honor.
b: Of King Asa the Plain says, "Then they lit a great fire for him, very great" (2 Chronicles 16:14), and of Jehoram, "His people lit no fire for him like the fire for his ancestors" (2 Chronicles 21:19). Radak says the burnings were of spices on the dead man's bed, and the Sages add that the household things he had used were burned. "Alas, lord!" is a funeral cry (compare 1 Kings 13:30, "Alas, my brother"). The promise is that Zedekiah will have the honors of a king at his death.

p: Lachish and Azekah were the last fortified towns holding out. A letter from Lachish shows the same days.
b: Lachish and Azekah guarded the roads from the coast into Judah. A set of letters written in ink on pottery pieces (ostraca) was found in the burned gate area of Lachish. Letter 4 says the writer is watching for the fire signals of Lachish "because we cannot see Azekah", which is usually taken to mean Azekah had already fallen. The same letters show officials and army officers under strain, and Letter 6 speaks of officials whose words "weaken the hands" (see 38:4). They are usually dated to the last months before Lachish fell.

p: The Hebrew for making a covenant is 'cut' (karat). This chapter shows why.
b: The Hebrew idiom for making a covenant is karat berit, "cut a covenant." It comes from the slaughter of an animal in the ritual (Genesis 15:9–18). In this chapter the idiom is acted out: the people "cut" their covenant before the LORD, and in 34:18 the LORD says he will treat the covenant-breakers as they treated the calf that was cut in two. The Plain keeps "cut" here, as in 31:31, so the ritual behind the word stays visible.

p: Zedekiah's release follows the law of the seventh year, and perhaps the Jubilee.
b: Three laws govern the release of Hebrew slaves: Exodus 21:2 (a Hebrew slave works six years and goes free in the seventh), Deuteronomy 15:12–18 (the same, with a gift on release), and Leviticus 25:10, 39–41 (release in the Jubilee: "proclaim release in the land for all who live in it"). The word "release" (deror) is the one in Leviticus. Nahum Sarna argued that Zedekiah's release was a seventh-year release that the people carried out under pressure of the siege. Others suggest a plan to bring more men into the army or to win God's favor.

a: a fellow Judean, his own brother
p: The law speaks of the Hebrew slave. Jeremiah's version adds 'Judean'.
b: Exodus 21:2 speaks of a "Hebrew slave", and Deuteronomy 15:12 of "your brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman." Jeremiah's report joins "Hebrew" with "a Judean, his brother" (yehudi, achiv). By Jeremiah's day the old word "Hebrew" for an Israelite slave is fading and "Judean" names the people left in the kingdom. The rule is the same: no one may keep a fellow member of the people as a permanent slave.

p: The same Hebrew verb is used for repenting and for going back to old ways.
b: Shuv, "turn", is Jeremiah's great word for repenting and for falling back. In 34:11 the people "turned" (back to slavery), in 34:15 they "turned" and did what was right (freeing the slaves), and in 34:16 they "turned" again and took the slaves back. The Plain keeps "turned around" each time so the reader can hear the same verb. The release was a real turn, and so was the reversal.

a: each of you must let go his brother
p: The LORD quotes the law about the Hebrew slave, but not word for word.
b: Deuteronomy 15:12 says: "He is to serve you six years, and in the seventh year you are to release him as a free person." Jeremiah's version puts the release "at the end of seven years" (see the variant) and "send him away from you, free." The old law counted six years from each slave's purchase (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12). The people in Zedekiah's day appear to have treated it as one fixed year for everyone. The LORD says this law was part of the covenant at the exodus, though the books of Exodus and Deuteronomy tie the law to the covenant at Sinai and in Moab.

a: you turned around and did what is right in my eyes
p: The people cut their covenant in the house that bears the LORD's name, and so broke it in front of him.
b: The oath was taken "before me in the house that is called by my name": the temple. Breaking it was therefore profaning the LORD's name (34:16), as Leviticus 19:12 says false oaths do. In the temple sermon the people stood in the same place and said, "We are safe" (7:10). The covenant here is a small version of the Sinai covenant: a promise made in God's house to do what he commanded long ago.

p: The LORD turns the word 'release' against them.
b: Zedekiah's people refused to proclaim release to their slaves, so the LORD proclaims a "release" to them: they are set free to the sword, disease and famine. It is a bitter play on the word deror. The Ketiv/Qere forms of "terror" in this verse are spelling variants (zeva'ah or za'avah) of one word, and it occurs also in 15:4; 24:9; 29:18. The Greek reads "scattering" (see the variant).

a: into the calf they cut in two
t: The cut calf and the oath ritual
p: Walking between the halves of an animal was a self-curse sworn at a treaty, and not only in Israel.
b: Genesis 15:9–18 shows the rite with Abram: the animals were "cut in two down the middle" and a smoking oven and torch passed between the pieces. In Aramaic treaty texts of the 8th century BC from Sefire, in Syria, the swearer says, "Just as this calf is cut in two, so may Mati'el be cut in two", which is the same idea. The hearer takes the oath on himself: if I break this, let me be cut like this animal. The verdict is that the parallel is real and well attested, though the Bible gives the rite a different meaning, since it is the LORD who passes between the pieces in Genesis 15. "Like" is added in the Plain; the Hebrew simply puts the men and the calf side by side.

p: The Hebrew sarisim can mean eunuchs or high officials.
b: Sarisim were palace officers, and in many places the word means men made eunuchs for service (compare Esther). In Judah it is used for officials of the court in general, as in 2 Kings 25:19 ("one court official who had been in charge over the fighting men"). The Plain says "court officials" and leaves the question of mutilation open. The list here includes every group that swore: the officials of Judah and Jerusalem, the court officials, the priests and all the people of the land.

a: food for the birds of the sky
p: The fate of the covenant-breakers matches the covenant curses.
b: Deuteronomy 28:26 is the curse: "Your corpses will feed every bird that flies and every wild animal, and no one will be there to chase them off." Jeremiah repeats it for the people of Judah in 7:33, 16:4 and 19:7. In Jeremiah 34 the curse comes from the covenant just broken. The calf cut in two, and the corpses left for birds, are one picture.

a: which has gone away from you
p: The release took place during the siege, and the army left for a time, which is why the slaves were retaken.
b: The Babylonian army "has gone away from" Jerusalem: the siege was lifted for a time when Pharaoh's army came north (37:5, 11). The timeline many scholars draw: the siege began in January 588 (2 Kings 25:1); the people freed the slaves during it; Pharaoh Hophra's army came and the Babylonians withdrew; the owners, feeling safe, took the slaves back; the Babylonians returned (37:8). Chapter 37 tells the lifting of the siege from another side.

a: in the days of Jehoiakim son of Josiah
t: Out of order in the book
p: This story is earlier than chapter 34. It is placed here to contrast the faithful Rechabites with the faithless slave owners.
b: Jehoiakim reigned from 609 to 598 BC. The Rechabites say they came into Jerusalem when Nebuchadnezzar "came up into the land" (35:11), probably during the Babylonian campaigns after Jehoiakim's revolt, about 599 to 598 (2 Kings 24:1–2). The book's order is thematic: chapter 34 shows people who broke a promise made to God, and chapter 35 shows a family that kept a promise made to their ancestor for more than two centuries.

p: A clan descended from Rechab, who held to a desert way of life. Their ancestor Jonadab backed Jehu's war on Baal.
b: 1 Chronicles 2:55 says they are "the Kenites who come from Hammath, father of Rechab's family." Jonadab (Jehonadab in 2 Kings) son of Rechab went with Jehu in the purge of Baal's worship about 841 BC (2 Kings 10:15–23). The family kept his rules: no wine, no houses, no fields or vineyards, but tents. Nehemiah 3:14 names a Malkijah son of Rechab as a ruler of a district. The Hebrew phrase in 35:19, "stand before me," is the common way to say "serve me" (Deuteronomy 10:8).

p: A 'man of God' was a prophet. Hanan had a room in the temple for his followers.
b: The room belonged to "the sons of Hanan." "Sons of" can mean members of a group, as in the "sons of the prophets" (2 Kings 2:3). Hanan, the "man of God," seems to have been a prophet with disciples who kept a room in the temple. The rooms around the temple were used by officials, priests and other groups, so the Rechabites are brought into the heart of the place and see its officials and servants.

p: The Rechabites' rule is their family's rule. Jeremiah does not tell anyone else to give up wine.
b: Jeremiah sets out wine to test the Rechabites, and they refuse. The story is often used to argue for total abstinence. The text does not do that. The LORD praises the Rechabites for obeying their father, not for avoiding wine, and he does not tell Judah to drink no wine; elsewhere wine is a gift of God (Psalm 104:15) and was part of temple worship. The rule is a sign of a particular way of life and of loyalty to a founder.

a: live in tents all your days
t: Why tents, no fields and no wine?
p: Readers disagree on the reason for the Rechabite rules.
b: The text gives only the stated purpose: "so that you will live many days on the land where you live as foreigners." Some scholars read the rules as a protest against the settled farming culture of Canaan (with its Baal worship), a desert ideal that Hosea 2:14 and Jeremiah 2:2 also admire. Others think they were the rules of a craft guild of traveling metalworkers (the Kenites are linked to smiths) or simply a clan's way of life. Jeremiah does not praise the way of life itself, only the obedience.

p: The Rechabites left the countryside for Jerusalem when raiders came.
b: 2 Kings 24:2 says the LORD sent raiding parties against Jehoiakim: "Chaldean raiders, Aramean raiders, Moabite raiders and Ammonite raiders." The Babylonian Chronicle for Nebuchadnezzar's sixth year (599/598 BC) says he marched into Hatti-land and sent out detachments that plundered the Arab tribes. People of the open country fled into walled cities, which is what the Rechabites say they did.

p: If a family obeys a human ancestor, how much more should a nation obey God?
b: The LORD's argument is from the lesser to the greater (qal vachomer in the later rabbinic term): the Rechabites keep the command of a human ancestor, long dead, who spoke only once. Judah ignores the command of the living God, who has sent prophet after prophet. The Hebrew word for "correction" is musar, which also means discipline and instruction (see 32:33).

p: The promise reaches beyond the siege: the family will always have someone who serves God.
b: "Will never be without a man standing before me" uses the same phrase as the promises to the king and the priests in 33:17–18. The Hebrew idiom "stand before" often describes service to a king or to God (Deuteronomy 10:8; 1 Kings 10:8). The Rechabites are not told they will keep their land or escape the siege; the promise is only that the family will go on. Later Jewish and Christian tradition made them a model of loyal obedience.

a: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah
p: The scroll was dictated in the year Babylon beat Egypt at Carchemish and became the great power.
b: Jehoiakim's fourth year is 605 BC (25:1, also called Nebuchadnezzar's first year). In that year Nebuchadnezzar defeated the Egyptian army at Carchemish on the Euphrates and took control of Syria and Palestine, as the Babylonian Chronicle records. The threat from the north, which Jeremiah had been announcing since 627, now has a name and an army. That is why the LORD says to write it all down: the words have a date.

t: What was on the first scroll?
p: The scroll held 'all the words' from Josiah's day to 605. Scholars disagree on which chapters those were.
b: The scroll covered 23 years of speeches (25:3). Views: (1) the scroll was the nucleus of the book, perhaps most of the poems of chapters 1–20 and 25; (2) it held mainly warnings about the foe from the north (chapters 1–6) and the oracles against the nations; (3) nothing can be said about its contents, and the story is itself a literary account of the book's origin. Whatever it held, the story is the book's own account of how it began, and of the second scroll's added words (36:32).

t: Baruch the scribe and his seal
p: A seal impression naming 'Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe' has no known find spot, and it is disputed.
b: In 1978 Nahman Avigad published a clay seal impression (a bulla) reading "Belonging to Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe": Berekhyahu is the full form of Baruch, Neriyahu of Neriah. In the same article he published a second impression, for "Yerahme'el the king's son" (compare 36:26). Both come from the antiquities market, not from a dig, so we do not know where they were found, and seals from the market can be forged. A second impression with the same Berekhyahu inscription is also known. In 2014 Yuval Goren and Eran Arie argued from laboratory study that the Berekhyahu impressions are modern. In 2016 Peter van der Veen, Robert Deutsch and Gabriel Barkay replied that those arguments do not hold, while granting that this does not prove the impressions are genuine. The question is open. Even if genuine, the seal would show that Baruch existed and was a scribe; it would say nothing more about the scroll.

p: The Hebrew word does not say whether Jeremiah is in custody, under a ban or ritually unclean.
b: The word atsur means shut up, held back or restrained. Jeremiah is not yet in prison (that comes in 37:15). Possible reasons: a royal ban after the temple sermon (chapters 7 and 26), a ritual reason that kept him from the temple, or a threat to his life. Whatever the cause, Baruch must speak for him, and what Baruch reads is only a scroll, not the prophet's voice.

t: The fast of the ninth month
p: A public fast in December 604 gathered the whole country in the temple at a time of crisis.
b: The ninth month is Kislev, November–December. The Babylonian Chronicle says that in Kislev of Nebuchadnezzar's first full year (604) he took Ashkelon on the coast, and some scholars connect the fast with that news. Jehoiakim had been loyal to Babylon since 605; the fast shows how frightened people were. The Greek has the eighth year, not the fifth (see the variant). A fast is a call to repent and to ask God for mercy (Joel 1:14; 2 Chronicles 20:3), which is why Jeremiah thought the people might "turn back" (36:7).

a: Gemariah son of Shaphan the scribe
p: Shaphan's family, who had helped Josiah, now hear Baruch read. A seal impression names a Gemariah son of Shaphan.
b: Shaphan the secretary read the law-book to Josiah (2 Kings 22:3–10). His sons were Ahikam (who protected Jeremiah, 26:24), Elasah (who carried Jeremiah's letter to the exiles, 29:3), Gemariah (here) and Jaazaniah (Ezekiel 8:11). His grandson Gedaliah governed Judah after 586 (39:14). A clay seal impression reading "Gemaryahu son of Shaphan" was found in 1982 in the City of David, in a burned layer of Jerusalem that goes with the Babylonian destruction (reported by the excavator Yigal Shiloh). Many scholars identify him with this Gemariah. The names are not rare, and some stay cautious.
r: 2 Kings 22:3; 2 Kings 22:10; Jeremiah 26:24; Jeremiah 29:3; Jeremiah 39:14; Ezekiel 8:11

t: The officials in the scribe's room
p: Several of these officials appear elsewhere in the book and in Kings.
b: Elnathan son of Achbor led the men who brought the prophet Uriah back from Egypt to be killed (26:22–23). His father Achbor was one of the men Josiah sent to the prophetess Huldah (2 Kings 22:12–14). Lachish Letter 3 mentions "Coniah son of Elnathan, the commander of the army", who went down to Egypt, and it is sometimes suggested that this is a son of the Elnathan here. That cannot be shown. Two officials, Elnathan and Gemariah, speak up for the scroll (36:25).

t: Jehudi, son of the son of 'Cushi'
p: 'Jehudi' means 'the Judean', and his great-grandfather's name, Cushi, means 'Cushite'.
b: Jehudi's name, "the Judean," and his great-grandfather's, Cushi ("the Cushite"), may point to foreign roots that were fully absorbed. Zephaniah's father was also named Cushi (Zephaniah 1:1). A Cushite also plays a key role in 38:7–13 (Ebed-melech). Such names are not proof of origin, though, and the text does not say why the family carried them.

t: The winter house and the brazier
p: Palaces had a warm winter house and a cool summer house. The ninth month is December.
b: The ninth month falls in November–December, the rainy, cold season in Jerusalem. The king sits in the winter house, with a fire of coals in a brazier (the Hebrew ach) in front of him. Amos 3:15 speaks of "the winter house" and "the summer house." The fire is the means by which he destroys the scroll in 36:23, and its location is part of the scene.

a: tore them off with the scribe's knife
t: Who cut the scroll, and what are 'columns'?
p: The Hebrew has only 'he tore'. English must choose Jehudi or the king. 'Doors' means columns of writing.
b: The verb has no named subject: "he tore it with the scribe's knife and threw it into the fire." The Plain supplies "the king," as most readers do, since 36:24 shows the king's unmoved reaction and 36:25 that he "burned the scroll." Jehudi, who was reading, may have been cutting off each section as the king ordered. The word for columns is delatot, "doors", the panels of a scroll of joined sheets. Radak says it means pages that open and close like doors, and notes that the Targum has "pieces."

a: they did not tear their clothes
t: Josiah tore his clothes; Jehoiakim burned the scroll
p: Josiah's household tore their clothes when they heard the law-book. Jehoiakim's household did not.
b: Tearing clothes was the sign of grief and repentance. When Shaphan read the law-book to Josiah, "the king tore his clothes" (2 Kings 22:11, 19), and Shaphan's son Gemariah and Achbor's son Elnathan, who now plead with Jehoiakim, belong to the same families (2 Kings 22:12). The writer of the story contrasts father and son: Josiah heard a book and repented; Jehoiakim heard a book and burned it. Jeremiah 22:15–16 says Josiah knew the LORD.

p: 'The king's son' may be a title for a royal official, not only a son.
b: The Hebrew ben hammelek is used both of real princes and of an office. Malkijah "the king's son" owns the cistern in 38:6. Seal impressions with "the king's son" are known. The bulla for "Yerahme'el the king's son" that Avigad published (see 36:4) has the same unprovenanced origin as the Baruch seal, so its link to this man is uncertain.

t: A second scroll, like second tablets
p: Moses broke the tablets and God wrote them again. Jeremiah's scroll is burned and written again.
b: In Exodus 34:1 the LORD tells Moses to cut two new stone tablets "like the first" after he broke the first. The shape of the story is the same: what a human act destroys, God has rewritten. Readers have also pointed to Isaiah 40:8, "but our God's word will stand forever." The king can destroy a scroll, but the LORD can have the words written again.

a: No one belonging to him will sit on David's throne.
t: A curse on Jehoiakim's line and his body
p: The promise did not come true in an obvious way. Readers explain it differently.
b: Jehoiakim's son Jehoiachin did sit on the throne, for three months (2 Kings 24:8). 2 Kings 24:6 says "Jehoiakim lay down with his ancestors", and 2 Chronicles 36:6 says he was bound to be taken to Babylon. Readings: (1) the throne passed in only a weak sense, since Jehoiachin was taken to Babylon and no son of his sat on it again (22:30); (2) Josephus says Nebuchadnezzar killed Jehoiakim and had the body thrown outside the wall (Antiquities, book 10); (3) the curse is a threat that Jehoiakim was unable to escape, and a critical reading holds it to be not literally fulfilled.

a: still more words, many like them, were added
t: The second scroll and the growth of the book
p: The story says the book grew. Scholars disagree on how much of the growth the story describes.
b: Jeremiah's second scroll has "more words, many like them." Many scholars take this as the book's own memory of how it grew from a single scroll into the large book we have, with the same words and many new ones added. The two editions of the book (the shorter Greek and the longer Hebrew) show that growth continued for a long time, as Tov argues. Others read the story as only one stage, and do not think the whole growth is there. Jewish tradition credits Jeremiah himself with writing the book (Bava Batra 15a).

p: One king, three forms of his name.
b: The king is called Jehoiachin in 2 Kings, Jeconiah in some verses and Coniah here and in 22:24, 28. Nebuchadnezzar took him to Babylon in 597 and made his uncle Mattaniah king, "and turned his name into Zedekiah" (2 Kings 24:17). Zedekiah is a son of Josiah (37:1), so he is Jehoiachin's uncle. The name changed from Mattaniah ("gift of the LORD") to Zedekiah ("the LORD is my righteousness") is a sign of Babylon's power over him.

a: Please pray for us to the LORD our God.
t: A king asks for the prayer he was told not to hear
p: Zedekiah asks Jeremiah to pray, though the LORD had told Jeremiah not to pray for this people.
b: The LORD told Jeremiah not to pray for the people (7:16; 11:14; 14:11), and even Moses and Samuel could not turn him (15:1). Zedekiah sends Jehucal and Zephaniah just the same. Earlier, King Hezekiah asked Isaiah for the same thing in a siege, and the answer was rescue (2 Kings 19:4). Zephaniah son of Maaseiah is the priest who also carried a message in 21:1–2 and was written to by Shemaiah in 29:25–29. The king asks for prayer and will not listen to the answer (37:2).
r: Jeremiah 7:16; Jeremiah 11:14; Jeremiah 14:11; Jeremiah 15:1; 2 Kings 19:4; Jeremiah 21:1

p: An Egyptian army came north in 588 and the Babylonians lifted the siege for a time.
b: The Pharaoh is Hophra (Apries), who ruled Egypt from 589 to 570 BC and is named in 44:30. Ezekiel 17:15–17 says Zedekiah sent to Egypt for horses and soldiers, and that Pharaoh's army would not save him. The Babylonians pulled back from Jerusalem to meet the Egyptians. Jeremiah says the Egyptians will go home and the siege will start again (37:7–8). We know of the outcome from Jeremiah's later chapters; the Egyptians did not break the Babylonian siege.

a: Even if you struck down the whole army of the Chaldeans
p: The LORD says the outcome is fixed even if the Babylonian army were destroyed.
b: The picture is a strong one: even a camp of wounded men would get up and burn the city. It shows that the siege is not just a military event but the LORD's sentence, so a victory over the army would not change the verdict. Compare 21:3–7, where the LORD says he himself fights against the city.

t: What was Jeremiah going to do in Benjamin?
p: The verb halaq means 'divide', but its sense here with 'from there' is unclear, and the Greek reads 'to buy'.
b: The verb halaq can mean "divide, share out" and the phrase is "to share a share from there among the people." Readings: (1) to claim a share of family land in Anathoth, which fits the story of 32:6–15; (2) to slip away, as if from a related root meaning "smooth"; (3) the Greek has "to buy from there among the people." The guard's charge of desertion in 37:13 shows how it looked to others.

a: You are going over to the Chaldeans!
p: The Hebrew 'fall to' means to go over to the enemy, to desert.
b: Nafal, "fall," with "to" means to go over to the enemy side. Irijah accuses Jeremiah of desertion. The charge fits what Jeremiah was telling the people to do (21:9; 38:2). Zedekiah uses the same verb of the Judeans who had already gone over (38:19). Jeremiah's reply is "A lie!" (sheqer), and the charge itself was false: he was going to Benjamin.

a: the lockup, the house of Jonathan the scribe
t: A private house made into a prison
p: Judah had no large prisons. A scribe's house was turned into a lockup.
b: The Hebrew calls it bet ha'esur, "the house of bonds", and says the officials "had made it into the prison." It had been the house of Jonathan the scribe, and the text says nothing about what it was used for before. The next verse speaks of "the house of the cistern" and "cells" (37:16); the text does not say whether these were the same building or another. Jeremiah's fear in 37:20 shows how bad the conditions were: "or I will die there." The royal courtyard of the guard was a much better place (37:21).

a: the house of the cistern, into the cells
p: The Hebrew names an underground pit-prison. The second word is rare.
b: Bor means "cistern, pit," a plastered hole used for storing water, and bet habbor is the cistern-house, a dungeon. Hachanuyot is a rare word, probably "cells" or "vaults." The Greek writes the second word in Greek letters (chereth) without translating it. Many days there almost killed him (37:20).

p: Jeremiah asks the king the question Moses gave for testing prophets.
b: Deuteronomy 18:22 says, "When the prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the thing does not happen or come true, that is a word the LORD has not spoken." Jeremiah's opponents had said Babylon would not come (compare 28:2–4; 14:13). Now Babylon had come, and they were not around to answer for it. Compare Jeremiah 28:9 for the opposite test, where a prophet of peace is known when his word comes true.

a: a round loaf of bread from the street of the bakers
p: A daily loaf from the bakers' street shows the siege has reached famine.
b: A round loaf (kikkar lechem) is a single loaf, apparently one portion. The ration lasted "until all the bread in the city was gone", which matches 2 Kings 25:3: "hunger gripped the city hard." The street of the bakers is named only here, so nothing more is known of it. The bread was given on the king's order for a prisoner.

p: Two of these four names are known from seal impressions found in the City of David.
b: Jucal (Jehucal) son of Shelemiah is the man sent to Jeremiah in 37:3. Pashhur son of Malkijah was sent by Zedekiah in 21:1 (he is not the Pashhur of 20:1). Two clay seal impressions from the City of David excavations led by Eilat Mazar match two of these names. One reads "Yehukal son of Shelemyahu son of Shovi"; Mazar found it in 2005 and reported it in Biblical Archaeology Review in 2006. The other reads "Gedaliah son of Pashhur"; it came from the same excavation, near where the first was found, and was announced in August 2008. Common names make an identification uncertain, but the names of both men and of their fathers match (and, for Jehucal, of his grandfather).

a: His own life will be his loot
p: Jeremiah gave this advice earlier, in the same words.
b: The advice in 38:2 repeats 21:9 in nearly the same words, with two differences: 21:9 says the man who goes out "deserts to" the Chaldeans (the verb nafal), and 38:2 ends with "and he will live", which 21:9 lacks. The last clause of both is the same: "his own life will be his loot." The "loot" (shalal) is a soldier's spoil, and a man's life is the only spoil he will take. As elsewhere in Jeremiah, the third calamity, deber, is rendered "disease." The same promise is repeated for Ebed-melech and Baruch (39:18; 45:5).

p: The officials call Jeremiah's advice treason. A letter from Lachish uses the same words for their own kind of talk.
b: "Weaken the hands" means to take away the soldiers' courage. Lachish Letter 6 says the officials' words "weaken the hands" of those they reach, the same phrase. Jeremiah's words may have looked like treason in war, and the officials put them in terms of the people's "welfare" (shalom) against their "harm." For Jeremiah the true welfare of the people lay in surrender. The disagreement is about which word of God to believe, and the story gives Jeremiah the last word.

a: the cistern of Malkijah the king's son
p: The cistern echoes Joseph's pit and the laments in Psalms and Lamentations.
b: A cistern at the end of the dry season holds only mud. Joseph was thrown into a pit: "It was a dry pit, with no water in it" (Genesis 37:24). The psalmist cries "I have sunk in the mud of the deep" (Psalm 69:2), and Lamentations 3:53–55 speaks of being put "in the pit." A Jewish tradition makes Jeremiah the author of Lamentations, and some readers hear this scene there. Christian readers have seen in Jeremiah's suffering a pattern for Christ's.

p: A foreigner from the far south is the one man who acts to save Jeremiah.
b: Ebed-melech means "servant of the king" and may be a title. He is a Cushite (from Nubia, today's Sudan and southern Egypt) and a sarîs, a court official (the Greek has only "Abdemelech the Ethiopian"). He speaks to the king in the Benjamin Gate while the Judean officials sit still. His rescue of Jeremiah is rewarded in 39:15–18. Isaiah 56:3–5 later welcomes foreigners and court officials into the LORD's house.

p: Thirty men seems many for lifting one man. The Hebrew and Greek agree on the number.
b: The Greek has thirty too. The number may reflect the need to overcome opposition from the officials, to carry out a weak and muddy man, or to have enough men to stand against the guard. No witness read for this part has another number.

p: The rags were padding so the ropes would not cut into Jeremiah's body.
b: The Hebrew is "under the joints of your hands," a rare term that means the armpits. Ebed-melech lowers old rags and clothes first. This small gesture of care shows what Ebed-melech was: a man who thought of the thing that would hurt a weak man being hauled up.

t: The third entrance of the LORD's house
p: No one knows which entrance this was. The Greek turns the words into a name.
b: The third entrance is not identified; it may be a private passage between the palace and the temple (compare 2 Kings 16:18). The Greek writes the Hebrew words as a place name in Greek letters, as if it did not understand them. The place was chosen for secrecy: the king had to be able to meet the prophet without the officials knowing (38:24–27).

t: A king's oath and an earlier broken oath
p: Zedekiah swears by the LORD, but he had already broken an oath sworn by God to Nebuchadnezzar.
b: Zedekiah swears a life-or-death oath by the LORD. Ezekiel 17:13–19 and 2 Chronicles 36:13 say that Zedekiah had earlier sworn loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar by God's name and broke it. The oath to Jeremiah is kept in a narrow way: he does not kill him. But he is too afraid of the officials to follow his advice (38:19).

a: If you will go out to the officers
p: Earlier the LORD said Zedekiah would be captured. Here he is offered a way out.
b: In 32:4–5 and 34:3 Zedekiah will certainly be captured, but here, if he surrenders, the city will not burn and he will live. Readings: (1) the earlier words were conditional, as Jeremiah 18:7–10 teaches for all prophecies; (2) the offer is real but he cannot take it; (3) critical scholars see different stages in the tradition. Zedekiah's end, told in 39:4–7 and 52:7–11, shows he did not go out.

a: The men at peace with you have misled you
p: The palace women will sing a mocking song about the king's advisers, as Jeremiah himself once heard.
b: The Hebrew lines are a short taunt, "They misled you, they overpowered you, the men of your peace; your feet were sunk in the mud, they turned back." "The men of your peace" are his allies, as Jeremiah's own "trusted friends" watched for his fall in 20:10 and as Obadiah 7 says of Edom. The mud is the mud of Jeremiah's cistern: the king will sink where the prophet sank. The women in the palace are led out first (38:23); the fulfilment is told in 39:4–7.

a: I was letting my plea fall before the king
p: Jeremiah tells the officials what the king told him to say.
b: The plea about Jonathan's house was part of what he had said to the king (37:20), so what he tells the officials is true, but not the whole truth. The king had ordered him to say this, and the text says the officials "said nothing more to him, for the matter had not been overheard." Readers have debated whether keeping silence under orders to protect his life is lying. The text itself does not comment.

a: And it happened, when Jerusalem was captured
p: The Hebrew sentence continues in 39:3, after two verses about the siege.
b: The Hebrew of 38:28 ends with "and it happened, when Jerusalem was captured" and then goes on to 39:1–2 and picks up the thread in 39:3 (the officials of Babylon sit in the Middle Gate). The Greek chapter ends at "until the day Jerusalem was captured." The Plain keeps the unfinished clause with three dots. Part 39–45 tells what follows.
